<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:1}
		Eq.~(\ref{eq:2}) has a unique root satisfying $0<r_{i,i}<1$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:2}
		The recursive sequence (\ref{eq:4}) is monotonically increasing and bounded above by 1. Thus, we have $\lim_{n \to \infty}x_n=r_{i,i}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We now state Rouché’s theorem \cite{adan2006application}, which we will need to prove Lemma \ref{lem:1}.
		
		\begin{theorem}[Rouché’s Theorem]
			Let the bounded region $D$ have a simple closed contour C as its boundary. Let $f(z)$ and $g(z)$ be analytic both in $D$ and on $C$. Assume that $\lvert f(z) \rvert < \lvert g(z) \rvert$ on $C$. Then $f(z) - g(z)$ and $g(z)$ have the same number of zeros in $D$; all zeros are counted according to their multiplicity.
		\end{theorem}
		Let $ f(z)=\lambda+i\mu z^{b+1}$, $g(z)= (\lambda+ i\mu + (c-i)\alpha) z$, and $h(z)= f(z) - g(z)$. Accordingly, $f(z)$ and $g(z)$ are analytic on the unit disk, $ \lvert z \rvert \leq 1$. In addition, $\lvert f(z) \rvert <\lvert g(z) \rvert$ on the unit circle, $ \lvert z \rvert = 1$. 
		
		Thus $h(z)$ has one zero, as does $g(z)$, on the unit disk. As a result, Eq.~(\ref{eq:2}) has a unique root in (0,1).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Let the bounded region $D$ have a simple closed contour C as its boundary. Let $f(z)$ and $g(z)$ be analytic both in $D$ and on $C$. Assume that $\lvert f(z) \rvert < \lvert g(z) \rvert$ on $C$. Then $f(z) - g(z)$ and $g(z)$ have the same number of zeros in $D$; all zeros are counted according to their multiplicity.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We use induction to prove that the recursive sequence $\{x_n\}$ is monotonically increasing, i.e.,
		\begin{align*}
			x_{n+1}> x_{n }, \quad \text{for} \quad n\in \mathbb{N}. 
		\end{align*}
		For the case $n=0$, we have 
		\begin{align*}
			x_{1} = p \geq x_{0}.
		\end{align*}
		Thus, the statement holds in the case $n=0$. Assume that the statement holds for some positive integer $k$. Then,
		\begin{align*}
			x_{k+2}-x_{k+1}= q( x_{k+1}^{b+1}-x_{k}^{b+1}) > 0,
		\end{align*}
		since $x_{k+1} > x_k$ by the induction hypothesis. Hence, $x_{n+1} > x_n$ for all positive integers $n$. 
		
		Next, we use induction again to prove that the sequence is bounded above by 1. The hypothesis holds for $n = 0$ since $x_1 = p < 1$. Assume that $x_k < 1$ for all positive integers up to $k$. Then,
		\begin{align*}
			x_{k+1} = p+ q x_{k}^{b+1} < p+q < 1.
		\end{align*}
		Hence, $x_n < 1$ for all positive integers $n$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
